stops.name: Bollingen, the Tower and the carved stone
stops.campa: Jung takes the Chilean up the lake to Bollingen, to the round tower of stone he raised with his own hands, a dwelling without electric light where the old man lives as in the Middle Ages. In the garden stands the great cube Jung cut and carved himself, the Bollingen Stone, its faces graven with the little cloaked Telesphoros and Latin mottoes of the alchemists. For Serrano, the seeker of the sacred mountain and the interior stone, this hewn cube by the water is a revelation: the Self made mineral, the philosopher's stone set down at the lake's edge.

stops.name: Küsnacht, the last letter of Jung (14 September 1960)
stops.campa: From the house on the lake, near the end, Jung writes to the Chilean a letter that Serrano will guard as a testament: a document, he says, of great importance, in which the old man sets down his last thoughts on the nature of the world and of his own labour. In it Jung tells how the ancient Gods never died but sleep in us, how Wotan in reality retained his vitality and returned; how man is a top animal exiled on a speck of planet, cosmically isolated, not the master in his own house. And at the last he confides that he guards his light and his treasure: most precious not only to himself but to the darkness of the Creator, who needs Man to illuminate his Creation. The corpus keeps this letter upon its own chain.
stops.quote: I am guarding my light and my treasure, convinced that nobody would gain and I myself would be badly, even hopelessly injured, if I should lose it. It is most precious not only to me, but above all to the darkness of the Creator, who needs Man to illuminate his Creation.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung to Miguel Serrano, Küsnacht, 14 September 1960; in A Record of Two Friendships

stops.name: Montagnola, 'the Hermetic Circle', 22 January 1961
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of January, snowflakes drifting past the window, Serrano takes lunch with Hesse at Montagnola. When the Chilean marvels at his fortune in having met both the poet and the sage, Hesse answers that nothing happens by chance: that here only the right guests meet, that this is the Hermetic Circle. The words seal the whole meaning of Serrano's wandering: the friendships were no accident but a summons, a gathering of the initiated across the mountains and the ice. It is one of the last of their meetings; the poet has months to live.
stops.quote: Nothing ever happens by chance. Here, only the right guests meet. This is the Hermetic Circle.
stops.quote_source: Hermann Hesse to Serrano, Montagnola, 22 January 1961; in A Record of Two Friendships

stops.name: Küsnacht, the death of Jung, 6 June 1961
stops.campa: On the sixth of June the sage dies in his house at Küsnacht, and a great storm is said to break over the lake, lightning striking the poplar in his garden. Hesse follows him into the ground within two months. Serrano, bereft of both his fathers of the spirit, gathers the letters and the last conversations and begins the book that will carry their voices, C.G. Jung and Hermann Hesse: A Record of Two Friendships. Through him the two old men of the Swiss lakes speak on. He is now the sole surviving guest of the Hermetic Circle.
stops.quote: Nobody understands what I mean. Only a poet could begin to understand.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung to Serrano; in A Record of Two Friendships

stops.name: Belgrade, ambassador to Yugoslavia
stops.campa: From India the Republic sends him to the Balkans, ambassador to Tito's Yugoslavia at Belgrade where the Danube takes the Sava. He moves through the marshal's court, arranging Tito's own visit to Chile, a servant of the state by day and a mythographer by night. In the old crossroads of empires, on the fault between the Latin and the Slav worlds, he reads the landscape as ever through his myth. The diplomat's postings are, to him, stations of a single pilgrimage; every capital is a stop on the road up the Mountain.

stops.name: Vienna, envoy on the Danube, credentials to Bulgaria
stops.campa: His last and longest embassy is Vienna, whence he serves also to Bulgaria, presenting his credentials at Sofia in December of 1965, and represents Chile before the Atomic Energy Agency and the industrial-development body on the Danube. In the imperial city of Vienna, in the heart of the German-speaking world he has revered since Barros Arana, he seeks out the old surviving figures of the defeated cause, gathering them into his private mythology. Here, on the great river, the ambassador spends the last years before the recall that will end his diplomatic life.

stops.name: Sofia, credentials to Bulgaria, 10 December 1965
stops.campa: On the tenth of December he presents his credentials at Sofia as Chile's first extraordinary ambassador to Bulgaria, one more capital of the socialist East added to his circuit. He crosses the Iron Curtain as a matter of protocol, moving between Vienna and the Balkan courts. In these grey Cold-War capitals the mythographer keeps his double life intact: the correct envoy of a small Andean republic, and, beneath, the reader of ley-lines and hidden orders, forever mapping the visible embassies onto the invisible geography of his cosmos.

stops.name: Madrid, the surviving figures of the defeated cause
stops.campa: Out of Vienna the ambassador travels to the corners of Europe where the vanquished of the war have gone to ground: to Madrid and the Iberian exile, seeking out the old aviators and soldiers of the lost cause, Rudel and Skorzeny, Degrelle in his Spanish refuge, Hanna Reitsch. In them Serrano reads not defeated men but survivors of a cosmic reverse, keepers, in his mythology, of the same secret withdrawn beneath the poles. He gathers their stories into his private cosmos, threads of the golden cord. The historian sees fugitives; the mythographer sees Hyperboreans in exile.

stops.name: Montségur, the pog of the Cathars, Languedoc
stops.campa: In the Languedoc he climbs the pog of Montségur, the last citadel of the Cathars, where in 1244 more than two hundred Perfect Ones walked singing into the crusaders' fire rather than recant. For Serrano this scorched mountain is the western Kailash, a pole of the Grail. He tells how, among the ruined walls, great arms of stone opened and a transparent emanation came to him: a sublime, superhuman love that moved him to tears. The mountain of the heretics answers the mountains of the ice and the Himalaya. This stop faces Molay's Templars and the corpus's own heresies.
stops.quote: Large arms of stone opened and a transparent emanation came to me, of sublime, superhuman love, which moved me to tears.
stops.quote_source: Miguel Serrano, on Montségur; in El/Ella, Book of Magic Love

stops.name: Montségur, the Grail as the stone of Lucifer's crown
stops.campa: On the burnt summit Serrano completes his gnosis of the Grail. The stone the Cathars hid, he teaches, is no cup but a jewel fallen from the crown of Lucifer, Earendel, the morning star, struck loose in his combat in the heavens when Hyperborea and Atlantis were destroyed. The Cathars were the guardians of the green ray, the keepers of Solar Kristianity, and their pyre at Montségur is a station of the same defeat that runs through the Templars, the vanquished of the war, the interior Kailash. All his mountains are one mountain, and the Grail-stone waits within it.
stops.quote: The Grail, hidden by the Cathars, was a jewel fallen from the Crown of Lucifer, broken in his combat in the heavens, when Hyperborea and Atlantis were destroyed.
stops.quote_source: Miguel Serrano, NOS, Book of the Resurrection

stops.name: Santiago, the recall from the diplomatic service
stops.campa: With the election of Salvador Allende the mythographer is stripped of his embassy and dismissed from the service of the state he has represented for seventeen years. The public career is over. Serrano reads the recall not as a defeat but as a release into his true vocation: from now on he will build in the open the cosmos he has carried since the ice. The diplomat becomes wholly the myth-maker. He withdraws from the Republic's business to the labour that will fill the remaining forty years: the writing of the Golden Thread.

stops.name: Montagnola, the exile in Hesse's own house
stops.campa: Dismissed, Serrano crosses again to Switzerland and settles above Lake Lugano in the Casa Camuzzi at Montagnola: the very house where Hermann Hesse had lived and written for twenty years. In the poet's rooms the pilgrim closes a circle: the man who first climbed to Hesse's door in 1951 now keeps that door himself, tenant of the Hermetic Circle's own address. Here, in the years of exile, he broods over the great books to come, the Grail and the poles and the resurrection gathering toward the Cordón Dorado.
